claims.text: Manual sample prep consumes 30% of technician time in contract labs
claims.quote: Contract labs spend 30% of technician time on manual sample prep

check.reason: No independent source gives 30% for contract labs. Published estimates for sample prep are higher, at roughly 50–60% or more of analysis time, but they measure analysis time in analytical labs rather than technician time in contract labs. The deck's 30% is therefore plausible and possibly conservative, but not confirmed.

title: LabLoop

brief.headline: Dig deeper, not yet a meeting: the traction numbers are unverified and the burn and headcount do not reconcile, while the 'no direct competitors' claim is already contradicted.
brief.summary: LabLoop sells robotic sample-prep automation to contract labs. It claims 26 paying customers, $38k MRR ($456k ARR) and 40% month-on-month growth since January, and is raising a $3M seed at a $15M pre-money. None of the core traction figures could be checked publicly: the customer count, MRR and growth are all unverified, and the only public 'LabLoop' result is unrelated. What did not hold up: 'no direct competitors' is contradicted by Metrohm, Labman and Curiox; the $4.1B TAM is above the $2.2-3.1B range for all US lab automation; and $90k monthly burn across 25 people is only $3.6k per head. The $15M pre-money is 33x ARR and 3.0x the year-3 forecast, and the forecast is supported only by the deck's own TAM-times-share arithmetic. This is a deck-only review, so nothing has been tested with the founders yet.
strengths: Claimed $38k MRR across 26 customers is about $1.5k per customer per month, which is plausible for a lab-automation subscription if the contracts are real
Seed ask of $3M at the stated $90k burn would give about 33 months of runway, which is ample if the burn is accurate
Problem framing is plausible: the 30% technician-time figure may even be conservative against published sample-prep estimates of 50-60% of analysis time
Team pitch pairs a Thermo Fisher industry operator (CEO) with a robotics PhD (CTO), though neither claim is verified

red_flags.text: 'No direct competitors' is contradicted: Metrohm, Labman and Curiox already sell robotic sample-prep to contract labs and CROs, and Opentrons sells at about $16k-$25k. The '10x cheaper than incumbents' claim holds only against some incumbent models, and the deck gives no LabLoop price. Differentiation is unproven, and a founder who overstates here is a credibility concern.

Traction is entirely unverified and the growth claim is aggressive. 40% monthly for 10 months is 28.9x, implying only about $1.3k MRR in January. The company has no public footprint to corroborate 26 customers or $38k MRR, and it is unclear whether these are paying recurring contracts or pilots.

Burn and headcount do not reconcile: $90k monthly burn with 25 people is only $3.6k per person, below realistic fully loaded cost. Either the team size or the burn is wrong, which undermines the stated 33-month runway.

Valuation looks stretched: $15M pre-money is 33x current ARR of $456k and 3.0x the year-3 revenue forecast of $5M. That forecast is validated only by the deck's own TAM-times-share maths, not by a bottom-up build.

The $4.1B contract-lab TAM looks inflated against $2.2-3.1B estimates for all US lab automation. It would need a broader definition (services, consumables) or an outlier report at about $4.46B. The 2% share target, which rests on that TAM, has no support.

questions: Who did your 26 customers evaluate you against (Metrohm, Labman, Opentrons, Hamilton, Tecan), why did they choose you, and what is your price versus theirs?
Walk us through MRR month by month since January, by customer. Which of the 26 are paying recurring contracts rather than pilots, and how many have renewed?
What is the real headcount split (full-time, part-time, contractors, offshore) and the true monthly burn, given that $90k across 25 people is only $3.6k per head?
What bottom-up build (customers x ACV, sales capacity, pipeline) gets you to $5M in year 3, and why is a 33x ARR valuation justified?
What is your source and definition for the $4.1B TAM, given that independent estimates for US lab automation are $2.2-3.1B?
